analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for custody officers to ignore medical distress in their care.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime for federal law enforcement officers, Bureau of Prisons staff, and U.S. Marshals to negligently fail to get medical help for a person in their custody who shows medical distress — including trouble breathing — if the person suffers unnecessary pain, injury, or death. Officers who violate it could face up to a year in prison, a fine, or both. Inspectors General would be required to investigate every such incident and refer negligent cases for prosecution, agencies would have to train staff on responding to medical distress, and state attorneys general could sue for relief. It is named for Andrew Kearse, a man who died in law enforcement custody in New York in 2017 after repeatedly telling officers he could not breathe.
analysis.who_benefits: People in federal custody — people under arrest, immigrants or defendants held by the Marshals, and people imprisoned in federal prisons — who are entirely dependent on officers for medical help. Their families would also gain a confidential complaint process and required investigations after any incident.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in federal custody and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal law enforcement officers, Bureau of Prisons staff, and U.S. Marshals to provide or obtain immediate medical attention for anyone in their custody who shows medical distress, including breathing difficulties.
Creates a new federal crime, punishable by up to one year in prison and a fine, for negligently failing to act when that failure causes unnecessary pain, injury, or death.

Requires Inspectors General to investigate every incident where someone in custody suffered unnecessary pain, injury, or death after medical help was withheld, and to refer negligent cases to the Attorney General for prosecution; also creates a confidential complaint process and mandatory training.
Allows state attorneys general to bring civil suits for equitable and declaratory relief on behalf of residents harmed by such violations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement officers and prison personnel, who face a new criminal penalty for negligent failures, and the agencies that employ them, which must provide training on responding to medical distress.

drawbacks.text: The bill uses a negligence standard — the lowest level of fault — rather than requiring intent or recklessness, so officers could face criminal charges over split-second judgment calls in fast-moving situations; an honest supporter would acknowledge this raises the risk of punishing honest mistakes alongside genuine indifference.
The maximum penalty is one year in prison, a relatively short term that limits how much the criminal exposure deters serious failures.

People in custody can already sue under existing civil rights law for deliberately indifferent failure to provide medical care, so the bill adds a criminal track and investigations on top of a system that already addresses the harm, adding costs and complexity without removing the constitutional avenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: federal custody populations are vulnerable by definition, and the bill creates a clear duty to call for medical help plus guaranteed investigations. The main cost is borne by officers who face criminal liability under a negligence standard that can reach ordinary mistakes, and the one-year maximum sentence makes the punishment modest relative to the harm of a death in custody. A reasonable bill overall, with design choices (negligence, short penalty) that critics could fairly contest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 11, 2021 by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with six original cosponsors — five of 48 Senate Democrats and one of two Senate independents — and was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken: the Judiciary Committee held no vote on the bill, the full Senate never debated or voted on it, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Democrats held the Senate majority during this period, so the bill died without action in a chamber controlled by the sponsor's own party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement and prison personnel are better off because the bill died — they avoid a new criminal duty and penalty for ignoring medical distress — while people in federal custody remain without the protections the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred; the only recorded support came from Democrats and independents, and the bill died in committee without any vote to show where the Senate stood.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and corrections personnel
industries.note: The bill would create a new federal crime — up to a year in prison — for negligently denying medical help to someone in custody, plus mandatory investigations and training. Their interest in avoiding this exposure runs against the accountability the bill would give to the people they hold.

industries.industry: Federal agencies (Bureau of Prisons, Marshals Service, federal law enforcement agencies)
industries.note: Agencies would bear training costs and face required Inspector General investigations and prosecution referrals after custody deaths. The investigations add scrutiny but also institutional overhead.
